purpose: An operator-invoked prompt (disable-model-invocation: true, correct-SKILL.md:4). It tells an agent to mine a repo's history for repeated mistake classes and make each one impossible at the highest structural level. It then has the agent prove each new check against a real past mistake and keep a rule-to-enforcer table (correct-SKILL.md:9, 15, 17-30). The reply format is each class with its evidence, the level chosen, and why no higher level worked (:32).
mechanism:
The skill is prose only. 33 lines with no scripts, agents or dependencies. I read all three files in full. The digest says SKILL.md is 2,445 bytes, which I did not re-measure. Mechanisms, in order:

1. Framing (:9-11). Every contributor is assumed to be an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. The repo should be designed so that a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.
2. Mining (:15). The sources are recent commits, reverts, review comments, agent instruction files, and comments that explain workarounds. The class threshold is "happened twice". It gives no query method, no window size, and no way to separate a repeat from a coincidence.
3. Four-level ladder (:19-22):
   - L1 architecture: single owner for each piece of state, one supported path per task, hidden internals so the wrong import fails, one source of truth in place of hand-synced lists, and deletion of old paths and dead code an agent would copy.
   - L2 types, then a lint or CI check "whose error names the file, type, or function to use instead". If the pattern is already common, the check fails only on additions (a ratchet).
   - L3 tests. Fix or delete any test that would still pass if every function it calls returned nothing.
   - L4 docs and agent rules, "last, only for judgment calls. Nothing fails when an agent skips them."
4. Fix and prove (:26). Fix the most frequent classes now, one commit each. Prove each new check fails on a real past mistake. Run the same command locally and in CI. Exceptions go on the offending line with a reason, an expiry date, and a human's approval.
5. Rule table (:30). The agent instruction file holds a table pairing each rule with its enforcer. On an operator correction, fix the mistake and add the rule. A rule that already existed with no enforcer counts as a repeat, and the fix goes at the highest level in the same change. Drop a rule once its mistake can't happen.
6. Re-run trigger (:3 description: "Repeat this each time the operator corrects you"). The body at :30 covers the same case. No hook or session-end trigger exists, so it depends on the agent or operator noticing.

The parent principle, encode-lessons (pstack-encode-lessons-SKILL.md), is the same idea at lower resolution. It supplies "pick the strongest mechanism" (:19), a capture/route/close-the-loop cycle (:23-26), and a routing of one-off to brain note, recurring to skill or lint, and systemic to principle. /correct adds the class threshold, the proof-on-a-past-mistake step, the exception format, the rule table, and the rule-drop step. The PR body says the skill body keeps the "source prompt's content and order", and that the edits are only format and wording (PR-494-body.md:6). Provenance beyond that is not given.
fit_and_overlap:
Standing note. The digest says the incumbents' coverage is not verified and defaults to REFUTED. I read only the three candidate files, so every "covering incumbent" below is the digest's description and is unverified. No skill on this harness performs the whole sweep (digest :30).

Mechanism by mechanism:

1. Mine commits, reverts, review comments, instruction files and workaround comments into classes.
   - Nearest incumbents: memory feedback notes (1,095 fleet-wide, 144 for dotfiles, digest :15) and papercut (digest :14).
   - Memory feedback holds operator corrections as raw material, but nothing groups them by git history. The duplicate rule is "update the existing note", not "escalate".
   - Papercut covers tool and environment friction, not operator corrections of agent behaviour. Its dedup and rank-by-distinct-sessions ranking is the closest to a "class" threshold.
   - Verdict: no incumbent mines git history or review comments. Partial at best.

2. Class threshold "happened twice".
   - Papercut ranks by distinct sessions and has `family create/assign` for causal families (digest :14). That is a comparable threshold, but only for friction.
   - Memory has no threshold and updates in place.
   - For corrections: none.

3. Fix at the highest level, with the ladder architecture > types/lint > tests > docs.
   - rent-check RUBRIC E2 promotion ladder is "cheapest deterministic layer that fully covers" (digest :16). It is a cost-first rule, so it points the opposite way from /correct's strength-first rule.
   - The rent-check ladder covers context-file rules only, not repo architecture.
   - The CLAUDE.md root-cause rule ("no band-aid patches, one guard in the shared function") is prose with no enforcer (digest :18). It is a partial architecture-level nudge.
   - Papercut's "Cheapest remedy" dossier field is a third, also cost-first.
   - Verdict: partial for the hooks, permissions and lint layers. L1 architecture has no incumbent.

4. Each new check must fail on a real past mistake.
   - Papercut dossiers have "Planted negative" and "Pre-registered success measure" fields (digest :14), which are the closest analogue.
   - Hook tests (hooks/tests, 50 files) and tests/*.test.sh give a place to put such tests (digest :19).
   - rent-check E4 paper-tiger gates targets checks that never fire (digest :16).
   - None of these makes the proof step mandatory on a correction.

5. Same command locally and in CI.
   - The harness-tests.yml workflow names suites individually (digest :19), and harness-doctor.sh has about 31 checks. Whether the CI and local commands are the same was not verified.
   - Partial. This is a repo property, not a skill.

6. Exceptions carry a reason, an expiry and an approver.
   - None found in the digest. vendored-drift-check pins are a different thing. Unknown.

7. Rule-to-enforcer table in the agent instruction file.
   - HARNESS.md "Autonomy & permission model" is a prose-to-enforcer map for one section only (digest :20).
   - rent-check E1 classifies rules as redundant, advisory-only or backing-without-mention. That is the audit form of the same table, with proposed diffs and not a maintained table.
   - E5 obedience telemetry is only proposed.
   - Verdict: strong partial. rent-check audits what /correct tells you to maintain.

8. "Rule with no enforcer = repeat, so escalate in the same change".
   - Memory's duplicate doctrine does the opposite and updates the existing note (digest :15).
   - rent-check E1 and E2 flag advisory-only rules and promote them, but only when run (user-invoked).
   - The CLAUDE.md root-cause rule has no enforcer.
   - This is a genuine gap on corrections.

9. Drop rules once impossible.
   - rent-check verdicts include CUT and DEMOTE (digest :16), so partial coverage exists for context files.

10. Re-run on every operator correction.
   - No incumbent triggers this. The harness has no SessionEnd hook (digest :5). UserPromptSubmit exists and could carry a correction detector, but nothing here does that.
   - The "docs last" level is ce-compound into docs/solutions (65 files, digest :17). /correct would put docs at the bottom, whereas ce-compound makes the doc the primary output. That is a stance conflict, not a gap.

Ladder comparison:
- Against poteto (digest :6): 1 architecture/data structures, 2 lint rule or test so CI catches it, 3 skill or rule, 4 humans review. /correct splits poteto's level 2 into types, then lint, then tests. It also puts docs (poteto's level 3, "skill or rule") last and omits "humans review" as a level. It adds that lint errors must name the replacement and that tests must be non-vacuous. /correct's ordering is consistent with poteto's. The extra resolution is the only difference.
- Against encode-lessons (pstack-encode-lessons-SKILL.md:19): that principle orders unrepresentable state, then lint or banned API, then canonical helper, then runtime check. It has no test level and no docs level, though it sends "no/judgment" cases to a more prominent instruction (:17). /correct has no canonical-helper or runtime-check level. Its L1 architecture covers "one supported way" and so subsumes the helper. Runtime checks are not named. The principle also routes the one-off case to a brain note (:25), and /correct drops that, since the one-off decoy is simply not classed.
- Against this harness's rent-check E2: that ladder is cheapest-first (linter/CI, then PreToolUse hooks, then permissions), and it is for rules in context files. /correct is strongest-first and for repo code. This ordering conflict is the main design tension if the two are combined.

Placement options, from the digest (:32): vendor into skills-local/correct/ with UPSTREAM.md and user-invoked only, extract text into papercut or memory doctrine or CLAUDE.md, or do not install. The skill is about 0 always-loaded cost and has zero deps. The honest gap is the on-demand sweep over git history plus the escalate-on-repeat rule. Both are cheap to add, so extraction of a few sentences is likely cheaper than vendoring a 33-line file, but that is a fit judgment for the lead.
dependencies: None. There are no scripts, agents or external services. It assumes the target repo has git history, a CI or `make check`-style single command (PR-494-body.md:14), and an agent instruction file. The PR touched only SKILL.md, README.md and plugin.json (digest :24).
maintenance: Low. The file is 33 lines and was merged 2026-10-03, so it is new and pstack has since moved from 0.15.7 to 0.15.15 (digest :4). If vendored, it needs an UPSTREAM.md pin so vendored-drift-check.sh can watch it (digest :9, :32). The "do not retry" triggers are not defined for this component. The licence was not in the files I read, so it is unknown. The "keep the rule table" step creates ongoing upkeep in whatever file holds it. HARNESS.md-scale tables drift unless an enforcer checks them.
red_flags: What the author's PR verification establishes (PR-494-body.md:10-14): (a) validate-plugins passes, so the format is valid. (b) A sentence-diff against the source prompt shows all 29 sentences present and in order, so the skill is a faithful rewrite of that prompt. (c) Leak grep is a hygiene check only. (d) Two Opus 5.5 runs, one per input, in a 17-commit scratch repo with 3 repeated classes and 1 decoy. Both found all 3 classes and did not class the decoy. Both used L1 architecture for the status list and the storage internals, put CI on the local command, added the rule table, and used inline exceptions with reason, expiry and approver. Five re-planted past mistakes failed `make check` in both runs, and each error named the replacement.

What it does not establish: (1) There is no bare arm. Both arms are the doctrine (raw prompt vs skill), so the only thing measured is that the skill wrapper did not lose anything from the raw prompt (:14 "The skill version lost nothing"). It says nothing on whether the doctrine beats a model given only 'stop repeated corrections'. (2) n is 1 per arm, so no variance estimate. The runs 'differ only in design choices' (money type vs lint, 542 vs 1143 lines), which shows run-to-run spread exists but cannot be sized. (3) One scratch repo that the author built with a known answer. Mistakes were planted to be findable, so recall of 3 of 3 is a plausibility check, not a recall measure, and one decoy gives almost no precision signal. (4) The re-plant check is circular. The agent writes the check and the author re-plants the mistakes it was told about, so the five failing is close to what 'prove it fails on a past mistake' already asks for. (5) Only one model family (Opus 5.5) was used, and this harness's fixture arms are Sonnet. (6) The 'two arms differ' result was sized in lines, and fewer lines is not evidence of better enforcement. (7) The PR body is the author's own agent-written text (CURSOR_AGENT_PR_BODY markers), so the run details cannot be independently confirmed from it.

Class threshold 'happened twice' is stated with no method, and the skill has no defence against inventing classes. The aihero retro FAQ names that as retro's strongest criticism (digest :8). The scratch repo's one-decoy test is the only evidence against it.

The skill assumes a repo with a CI gate and typed code. For a dotfiles/harness repo whose enforcers are hooks and permissions, 'types' has no meaning and the ladder needs translation. The rent-check E2 ladder is the harness-native one.
Ladder ordering conflict with rent-check E2 (strongest-first vs cheapest-deterministic-first). Combining them without choosing would send agents two ordering rules.

'Fix the most frequent classes now, one commit each' has the agent make architecture changes unprompted in a sweep. This is behaviour-shaping, so any port needs the adversarial review the digest requires (:33).

The skill has no session-end or correction trigger, so 'repeat each time the operator corrects you' depends on the agent noticing, which is the obedience problem it is meant to solve. The harness has no SessionEnd hook (digest :5).

claims_to_verify.claim: Memory's duplicate doctrine updates an existing feedback note and does not escalate a repeated correction to an enforcer.
claims_to_verify.why_verdict_changing: This is the digest's basis for the 'rule exists with no enforcer = repeat' gap. If a memory-audit or rehook path already escalates, that mechanism is covered.

claims_to_verify.claim: A behavioural fixture with a bare arm, built from a git-history repo with planted mistake classes and decoys, can discriminate /correct from bare and from rent-check at n=3 with Sonnet.
